Timing the arrival of AGI as if it will be a discrete moment in time is a sub-optimal framing of the problem. We need to remember that full AGI isn’t necessary for noticeably harmful effects on society. Remember these three phrases:

Misspecification. 
Erosion of control.
Power seeking.

You will notice that 3/3 of these failures are humanity's fault, not AGI. It’s our responsibility to overcome misspecification of optimization objectives. It’s our responsibility to not become over-reliant on opaque assisted decision-making technologies. It’s our responsibility to understand and formalize what power seeking looks like in AI systems (we’re making progress on this).  

A lot of the damage will be done well before true AGI arrives, and certainly before the experts agree on whether it has arrived. The litmus test for AGI may very likely be self-proclamation of sentience coupled with unpredictable and equally impactful autonomous behaviors. 

Don’t wait for consensus among experts when what we are creating is poised to surpass all experts entirely.

comments.text: This is not true.  There are fundamental limits to computational complexity.  AGI isn't likely to solve P vs NP, for instance.  The only thing impressive is that it has a large memory capacity, so it can memorize wikipedia and recall it faster than a person.  The advances in AI geometry are completely separate systems that wouldn't work with an AGI, as written (and as stated by the authors).  But even then, after every advancement is made to unify all human knowledge, and after it keeps training itself, even if it became smarter than any human, it will plateau very quickly.  Computation has hard limits, and numerous other limits somewhere between soft and hard.  Having a graph of a vertical line going off seemingly into infinity is a total lie.  It will run up against a ceiling very quickly.  AI can't out perform math and physics.  By the time we have to shrink it does to put it into personal devices, it will be much dumber, too--again, fundamental limits.  Devices connected to a high speed internet connection will be much smarter than isolated ones (for people who like privacy--which is most people).  But I don't know what the limit is.  Is it 3x human intelligence, 5x, 10x?  Once it gets there, any additional gain will be very small, and likely only achieved through smaller optimizations.  And finally, that intelligence will rapidly have to change after we give it a body, since a massive amount of resources go into maintaining a body (energy, materials, and computation).  Again, I assume one connected to the internet (or the AI's version of the internet) will be much smarter than disconnected ones.  Then we have to worry about wars between rival AIs, and fractured internets (groups who refuse to join over fear or propriety), and other stuff we have yet to dream up.  As an aside, it'd be funny if we realize that we don't know how to make AI smarter than us, we just assume we can.  Maybe it'll plateau right around the smartest human person.  I'd like to believe we can, but it's hard to say what other limits we will hit in our pursuits.
